name: Carlos Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43, a senior developer leading cold-storage alarm software at a tech company, and I have a master’s degree. I use AI every day to draft checks but still compare alerts with a handheld thermometer; I know this system well. Mira works at a pharmacy counter, and our mortgage and two school-age children leave little spare cash after a roof repair, especially on my lower-than-usual lead pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a little AI can sort routine temperature alerts, but a freezer full of food needs a real thermometer reading. I use AI every day to draft code and compare each alert with the sensor trace before release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead the cold-storage software team and have a master’s degree, yet my pay is low for a lead. My wife Mira works at a pharmacy counter; a roof repair left our mortgage household, with two school-age children, under one month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reviewing freezer alarms and ask the warehouse staff which false alerts caused wasted trips. We would cancel the extra phone data plan and put 28 monthly toward school shoes while both wages continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious about the next repair bill, not the small AI helper. A fridge alarm can be reset; the mortgage still takes its payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which alarm was hardest to explain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A sensor near the loading door showed warm air each time a pallet came in, though the food stayed cold. I checked the handheld thermometer before changing the alert rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why stay at the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are few comparable lead jobs nearby and our children are settled in school. I have asked for better pay, but a request will not buy school shoes.

I use **AI daily** for code drafts, then compare sensor traces.
think: I earn **low lead pay** despite a master’s degree and team responsibility.
I have **under one month saved** after roof repairs and school costs.
do: **Keep reviewing** freezer alarms and ask warehouse staff about false alerts.
**Cancel extra phone data** and reserve 28 monthly for shoes while wages continue.
feel: **Anxious** about repairs and the mortgage despite mild AI.
S0.quote: A fridge alarm can be reset; the mortgage still takes its payment.
fieldNote: His **thermometer check** catches an alarm distorted by a loading-door draft.
Thin savings follow **roof repairs** and lower lead pay, not a lack of technical skill.

steps.text: Keep reviewing cold-storage alarms and warehouse false-alert reports
Cancel extra phone data and reserve 28 monthly for school shoes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AI can write alert code and answer warehouse calls, so people should know who is checking the food before anybody is cut. I would ask management how many engineers and pharmacy counter staff remain when the easy tasks move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my team may lose posts as AI handles routine checks, and Mira’s pharmacy counter could also lose hours to automated answers. I may keep a lead title but see my pay or hours cut, while our savings would not cover the mortgage for a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d learn a new AI method for comparing a warm sensor with nearby readings using old cases and fake warehouse names. I’d show the result to the team and ask the director for a written staffing plan; if my hours fall, I’d apply online for paid cold-chain lead openings and travel only when an interview and bill-covering wage range are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious that both incomes could shrink. I like using a tool, but I cannot code a second pay cheque into our bank account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test the comparison?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d use the loading-door alarm and five other cases where food stayed cold. If the AI cannot separate door air from food temperature, it has not earned a release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mira train for another role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That is her choice; I would not make a plan for her without asking. We would compare what the pharmacy offers with our mortgage before paying for any course.

say: I want **named food checks** before AI changes warehouse code and calls.
I want **staffing figures** for engineers and pharmacy counter staff.
think: I expect **developer posts** and Mira’s counter hours could shrink.
I fear my **pay or hours** could fall with less than one month saved.
do: **Learn AI sensor comparison** on old cases with fake warehouse names.
**Request written staffing figures** after showing the test to my team.
**Apply for lead work** online if hours fall; travel only for confirmed bill-covering interviews.
feel: **Anxious** by two income risks despite useful tools.
S1.quote: I cannot code a second pay cheque into our bank account.
fieldNote: His **new AI comparison** tests a real loading-door false alarm, not routine tool use.
He limits **interview travel** until a viable wage range is confirmed.

steps.text: Learn AI warm-sensor comparison on old cases with fake warehouse names
Apply online for paid cold-chain lead openings if hours fall
Travel only for confirmed interviews with bill-covering wage ranges

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write and check nearly all our alert code for less, and pharmacy advice could change too. Robots that handle warehouse food may arrive around 2031, but the thinking work reaches both our jobs first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead wage could end and Mira’s counter hours could shrink before we have a month of bills saved. A paid field role might carry us through the first years, but robots in 2031 could take hands-on checks too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the company now for a written date on lead roles and keep our old car rather than take a new payment. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my role ends, I’d apply for paid cold-store sensor checks only where vacancies exist and wages cover our mortgage and bills; I would call the lender before arrears if work takes time to find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed and awake at night. A warm sensor is easier to test than a family budget with no salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you do field checks yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have gone with warehouse technicians to compare sensors with a handheld thermometer, but I am not a licensed electrician. I would seek a paid supervised role, not take electrical jobs alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who could help with the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother could do school pickup for a confirmed interview if Mira is on shift. I would ask for that one day, not make her our default childcare.

say: I say **thinking AGI in 2028** reaches alert code and pharmacy advice.
I know **warehouse robots around 2031** come later than the first job shock.
think: I expect my **lead wage** and Mira’s counter hours could both fall.
I know **field checks** may pay briefly before capable robots arrive.
do: **Keep the old car** and request a written date for lead-role changes now.
**Apply** for supervised bill-covering checks after 2028 displacement as a bridge before 2031 robots; call lender before arrears.
**Ask mother for pickup** only if a confirmed interview clashes with Mira’s shift.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless** about two wages facing the fast date.
S2.quote: A warm sensor is easier to test than a family budget with no salary.
fieldNote: His **field option** is supervised, not an unsupported claim to electrician work.
The **lender call** is conditional on a slow search and is not tagged as income support.

steps.text: Keep the current car instead of taking a new payment
Apply for bill-covering supervised sensor work after 2028 loss as bridge before 2031 robots
Ask mother for pickup only if a confirmed interview conflicts with Mira’s shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years before full AGI in 2031 gives us time to teach people how to tell a bad sensor from warm air near a door. Robots for warehouse handling may follow around 2034, but software changes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn more of the physical checks while I still earn a developer wage. Mira and I need a buffer before then, and any training that cuts pay would defeat the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my manager for a paid monthly visit with a warehouse technician to compare two sensors with a handheld thermometer, and go only if the company approves. I’d save 110 monthly only after a raise is approved and both wages cover bills; if my developer role ends after 2031, I’d seek paid supervised sensor work only where vacancies exist and pay covers our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious but able to test the work. I need a real paid route, not a certificate that sits in a drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you write after the visit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The freezer reading, the handheld reading and whether the loading door was open. I would ask the technician what I missed before calling it experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the manager refuses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my lead duties and use old sensor logs on paid work time if approved. I would not call a refused visit a skill I have learned.

think: I could learn **physical sensor checks** while earning a wage.
I need an **approved raise** before building the household buffer.
do: **Join** approved paid monthly sensor visits; if refused, study old logs on approved paid time.

**Seek supervised field work** if displaced after 2031 and paid vacancies cover mortgage.
feel: **Anxious but testing** a paid field route.
S3.quote: I need a real paid route, not a certificate that sits in a drawer.
fieldNote: His field learning requires **approved paid visits** with a warehouse technician.
The **saving step** needs an approved raise and two continuing household wages before any monthly deposit is counted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade before full AGI in 2036 gives our children time to grow and us time to make the household buffer real. Robots for warehouse work may follow around 2039, three years after thinking AI reaches code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could become competent at field checks and save three months of bills if my pay rises, but I would not call physical work safe forever. Mira’s counter work may change too, so both incomes matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading the freezer-alert team and write a short guide to checking a sensor against a handheld thermometer, using no customer names. We’d save 150 monthly only if an approved raise and both incomes cover bills; if my developer job ends after 2036, I’d apply for paid supervised equipment-support roles only where vacancies remain and wages cover the mortgage and basic bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious now because the roof repair has left us with almost no reserve. A long deadline helps only if we actually put money aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would use the guide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A new developer and the warehouse worker who sees the alarm. I would ask both to try the steps and tell me which reading was unclear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a better lead job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a written paid offer that covers new housing and school travel. Few lead jobs are nearby, but I would not ask Mira and the children to move on a guess.

say: I want **household reserves** built before full AGI reaches code in 2036.
I know **warehouse robots around 2039** follow the earlier thinking shock.
think: I could build **three months saved** only after pay improves.
I know **both household incomes** could change as AI spreads.
do: **Keep leading alerts** and write a sensor-check guide without customer names.
**Save 150 monthly** only after approved raise while both incomes cover bills.
**Apply** for bill-covering supervised equipment work after 2036 displacement; move only for written offer covering housing and school travel.
feel: **Anxious now** because the roof repair emptied savings.
S4.quote: A long deadline helps only if we actually put money aside.

The **reserve goal** depends on a real raise and both household incomes, not just his senior title or a distant date.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my lead wage and Mira’s counter hours could shrink before we save a month of bills. A written job date, paid supervised sensor work covering the mortgage and one-day pickup help from my mother during a confirmed interview would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a sensor is safe to work on. I will not take electrical jobs alone just because I wrote the alert code.

headlineQuote: I will not take electrical jobs alone just because I wrote the alert code.
portrait: Carlos is a **43-year-old senior developer** with a master’s degree, below-usual lead pay and under one month saved.
He and Mira cover **two children** and a mortgage, after a roof repair drained cash.
He uses **AI daily** but tests freezer alerts against physical thermometer readings.
He seeks **paid supervised sensor work**, aware that warehouse robots may arrive later.
The **2028 case** threatens both his software pay and Mira’s counter hours.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut his lead pay and Mira’s hours before they rebuild savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **written job date**, bill-covering supervised field opening and conditional family pickup would help.
